source.author: stat
source.text: illi ad fata rapi atque illi iam occumbere leto, sic meritam Hypsipylen iterant, creduntque, nec irae fit mora, iamque faces et tela penatibus instant, vertere regna fremunt raptumque auferre Lycurgum cum Iove cumque aris; resonant ululatibus aedes femineis, versusque dolor dat terga timori, Alipedum curru sed enim sublimis Arrastus secum ante ora virum fremibunda Thoantida portans it medius turmis, et parcite, parcite!
source.text_original: illi ad fata rapi atque illi iam occumbere leto, / sic meritam Hypsipylen iterant, creduntque, nec irae / fit mora, iamque faces et tela penatibus instant, / vertere regna fremunt raptumque auferre Lycurgum / cum Iove cumque aris; resonant ululatibus aedes / femineis, versusque dolor dat terga timori, / Alipedum curru sed enim sublimis Arrastus / secum ante ora virum fremibunda Thoantida portans / it medius turmis, et 'parcite, parcite!
source.text_english: for some it is to be snatched off to doom and for some now to fall in death; thus they repeat that Hypsipyle has well deserved it, and they believe it. Nor is there delay for their anger: already torches and weapons press upon the household gods, and they roar that they will overturn the kingdom and carry off Lycurgus, torn away, with Jove and the altars; the house rings with women’s wailing, and grief, turned about, gives its back to fear. But Arrastus, high on Alipedum’s chariot, goes through the midst of the squadrons, bearing the Thoantian before the faces of the shouting men, and says: Spare, spare!
